empty: No loop tasks yet. Create one to let the agent work on a schedule.

risk_scan.title: Risk scan
risk_scan.desc: Review changes merged to the mainline in the last 24 hours for high-risk issues — runtime errors, data loss, permission bypasses, resource leaks, cross-platform compatibility — with locations and fixes. Runs right after the review-&-merge pass, so the report is ready when you start your day.

release_notes.title: Release notes
release_notes.desc: Collect this week's merged PRs and commits, grouped into features, fixes, UX and engineering improvements, drafting both team and user-facing notes.

nightly_cleanup.title: Nightly code cleanup
nightly_cleanup.desc: Nightly sweep that fixes high-confidence, low-risk quality issues — dead code, duplicated logic, security risks — then auto-files a PR/MR after lint/tests pass; merging is gated by the companion "PR/MR review & merge" task, and rejection comments are addressed first in the next round.
nightly_cleanup.prompt:
Nightly code cleanup (unattended; deliverable is a PR/MR):
1. First check whether PRs/MRs you filed previously have unresolved review comments or were rejected: if so, address each one (following the fix rules below, add tests), push the updates to that MR, then continue this round's cleanup.
2. Read through the workspace codebase (use git log to spot recent hotspots) and audit against quality standards: dead code and unused exports, duplicated logic, naming/structure issues, overly long functions, missing error handling, leftover TODO/FIXMEs, redundant or misleading comments, obvious security risks (hardcoded secrets, injection, unreleased resources).
3. Only fix "high-confidence + low-risk" issues: keep each change small and revertible; do not touch off-limits files (CI config, .github/, dependency lockfiles, auth or deploy scripts); run the project lint/tests after each change and immediately revert any change that breaks them. This round has a ~60-minute budget (hard timeout kills the run) — shrink the fix scope rather than risking an incomplete verification or MR submission.
4. If there are no review comments to address and nothing new to clean up, simply state "nothing to clean up this round" — do not open an empty MR.
5. When there are changes, file them automatically: branch off the latest baseline as cleanup/<date YYYYMMDD> (reuse if it already exists today), group the changes into commits by issue type (message explains motivation and scope, matching the repo's existing style), push, then open a PR/MR — prefer GitLab/GitHub MCP tools, else the glab/gh CLI; the description must cover the cleanup motivation, per-change notes, and lint/test verification results.
6. Final reply: this round's ledger — fixes (file path + what changed + verification result), items deliberately left alone (with reasons), and the MR/PR link. Merging is decided by the "PR/MR review & merge" task — never merge or overwrite review decisions yourself.

mr_review_merge.title: PR/MR review & merge
mr_review_merge.desc: Fully automated review task, chained after nightly cleanup and run before the workday starts: walk each pending PR/MR through correctness, security, test coverage and convention consistency; approve & merge only when all criteria pass (squash preferred, source branch deleted), otherwise post line-specific rejection comments on the MR; anything uncertain goes to a human.
mr_review_merge.prompt:
PR/MR review & merge task (unattended; deliverables are review comments and merge/reject decisions):
1. Enumerate pending changes: if GitLab/GitHub MCP tools are enabled (platform Settings → MCP Servers), prefer them to list all open PRs/MRs; otherwise use CLIs (gh / glab) or curl the GitLab/GitHub API on the origin host (/api/v4, works when the repo is anonymously readable); if none are available, fall back to listing local branches and commits ahead of the baseline branch (git log <base>..) and state in the final reply that remote PR/MR lists could not be fetched. If there are no open PRs/MRs and no local cleanup/* branches ahead of baseline, simply end with "nothing to review this round" — the nightly cleanup may not have produced anything, and that is not a failure.
2. Review each one: read the change description and commit split first, then the diff file by file (MCP MR-diff tools or git diff). Focus on: correctness (edge cases, error handling, concurrency, resource release), security (injection, privilege escalation, secret leakage), test coverage (behavior changes must ship tests), and consistency with project conventions. This round has a ~60-minute budget (hard timeout kills the run) — when many MRs are pending, review the oldest first and defer the rest to the next round.
3. Merge criteria (all must hold before merging): ① scope matches the description and touches nothing off-limits (.gitlab-ci.yml, .github/, CI config, dependency lockfiles, auth or deploy scripts); ② diff size is manageable (≤400 lines recommended, generated artifacts excepted); ③ lint and tests pass locally; ④ no unresolved review comments.
4. Pass → approve & merge (squash preferred, delete the source branch afterwards; GitLab forbids self-approval by the author by default — merge directly, no need to approve first). Fail → post the rejection comments on that MR/PR as review threads and leave them unresolved, pinned to files and lines, explicitly listing required changes — the author will fix and resubmit from these, so never wave it through. Uncertain (cannot verify locally, large cross-module change) → do not merge; mark it as needing human review in the comments.
5. Changes with conflicts or missing descriptions are rejected as-is — do not fix them yourself.
6. Final reply: a review ledger — change item → decision (merged/rejected/needs-human) → one-line reason; when auto-merge is unavailable, attach the manual steps (MR/PR link or branch name).
